desc:
A string is compressed with the rule k[text], which means that text is written k times in a row. The text inside the brackets may itself contain letters and further k[...] groups. Letters outside any group are written as they are.

Given a valid compressed string s, return the full decoded string. Every number is a positive integer and is always followed directly by '['; numbers can have several digits.

Examples: '3[a]2[bc]' decodes to 'aaabcbc', and '3[a2[c]]' decodes to 'accaccacc'.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters, digits and the brackets '[' and ']'; it is well formed
Every number k satisfies 1 ≤ k ≤ 300 and is immediately followed by '['; every group has non-empty text
The decoded string has at most 20,000 characters
hints: Decoding from left to right is easy until you meet a group. What do you need to remember when a '[' starts a new group?
When you enter a group, save the text built so far and the number in front of the bracket, then start collecting a fresh text for the group.
Use a stack. On '[' push (text so far, k) and reset the text. On ']' pop (prev, k) and set the text to prev + text * k. Digits build up k, letters extend the text.
editorial: A group can be nested inside another group, and the outer one can only be finished after the inner one. That is last-in, first-out, so use a stack. Keep the current text and the number being read. Digits update the number as k = 10*k + digit. When you read '[', push the pair (current text, k) on the stack and start with an empty text and k = 0.

When you read ']', pop (previous text, k) and replace the current text by previous + current * k. Letters are appended to the current text. At the end the current text is the answer. Each character of the output is created and copied only a bounded number of times per nesting level, so the work is proportional to the size of the output times the nesting depth in the worst case; with a 20,000 character output this is tiny. Space is O(output).
